recent_texts: Protests over Israeli raids in Daraa and Quneitra dominate the news as national unity. But scroll the comments and people are just as angry about fuel lines, crime, and getting through the day.

A $500 fine for a pothole-ridden road? Some say it is the only way to tame the chaos on the streets. Others ask why drivers pay for roads the state never fixed. The comments are split right down the middle.

Israeli incursions still top the list, week after week, and Suwayda anger is rising fast beside it. Media says 'outlaw groups'. Online, people sound far angrier. Diesel lines in Aleppo and Idlib are not helping.
Officials talk Bahrain visits and expos. People talk diesel lines, traffic fines, and Suwayda's highway still cut off. The anger online runs far hotter than anything in the headlines.

Winter is coming and so are the diesel lines. People are not just angry, they are mocking officials outright, some even tying the shortages to unequal treatment between regions. Exhaustion is turning into open sarcasm.

One settler's quote, 'Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, those are ours too,' and it is suddenly everywhere online. English-language users call it proof of what they already feared. Arabic comments have stayed quiet on this one, for now.

Explosions near al-Kiswah and Sahnaya, drones overhead, and no one agrees on anything. Some mock the government outright, some openly welcome the strikes, others say it is all a distraction. Causes still unconfirmed.

A new school curriculum drops the old 'Butcher of Arabs' label for Jamal Pasha and changes how women are shown. Some mock it as one bias replacing another. Others defend the changes as reflecting Syria's diversity.
